newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Return to mining roots seen lifting Anglo. [corrected 14:12 gmt]
newsitem.headline: Return to mining roots seen lifting Anglo. [corrected 14:12 gmt]

text.p: Shedding peripheral businesses and streamlining mining operations would draw foreign investor interest to Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd and offer better share returns, analysts said on Wednesday.

"The group would have a broader international exposure than it does at the moment. Some investors might prefer the smoother earnings provided by having industrial interests," said John Clemmow, investment analyst at Investec Fergusson Brothers.

"But the trend internationally is that foreign investors like to see focus on what is believed to be core competency. It is my feeling that a refocus of Anglo onto its core business would be positive for the share," he added.
Anglo shares were trading at 292.50 rand per share at 1345 GMT.

Responding to a report in The Financial Times, Anglo said on Monday it was reviewing its assets and structure, but stressed that any decisions were hampered by South Africa's rigid foreign exchange controls and other obstacles.
The Financial Times said that Anglo had launched a strategic review which may lead to the disposal of non-core assets.

"Anglo is largely the way it is a result of exchange controls and it is clear that once they go, Anglo will look to dispose of non-mining assets and concentrate on being a big mining company," Clemmow said.
Anglo recently sold the bulk of its 47.4 percent stake in Johnnies Industrial Corp Ltd to the National Economic Consortium, a grouping of 50 black economic interests.
Earlier this year Anglo took a stake in Lonrho Plc with an eye, analysts said, to snapping up its mining interests when the British group unbundled.
Analysts agreed that by selling non-core operations, Anglo could be stocking a war chest for expansion and acquisition -- particularly within Africa.

"Specifically, Anglo has a role in Africa. Anglo already has vast resource projects in Zaire, Zambia and Mali. Any sale of non-core assets can generate cash to develop these properties," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.
Anglo has already allocated Africa around 218 million rand for capital spending in the current financial year on mining exploration alone.
But the Anglo group, with its vast offshore cash resources belonging to sister companies De Beers and Minorco SA suffered less from exchange controls than other local companies, analysts said.

"Worldwide, Minorco and De Beers both have substantial offshore balance sheets already. Anglo does not want to remain trapped in a hot-house economy. It is important that exchange controls go for them, but it is not critical," Clemmow said.
First National Bank Corp, in which Anglo and associated companies including De Beers hold 26.1 percent, and Southern Life are included in the non-core assets set for disposal, analysts said.
"We feel that Anglo is open to offers for what it calls non-core businesses. They are for sale if the price is right," Clemmow said.
